title: General, predictive functionalization of a chosen unactivated C–H bond in a complex molecule

concept.text: The proposed innovation would let a chemist select an unactivated carbon–hydrogen bond within a complex molecule and predictably transform that site while preserving the molecule’s other useful features. The central challenge is choosing among competing C–H bonds and functional groups: the desired reaction must occur at the selected position, avoid unwanted transformations elsewhere, and control stereochemistry where it matters. The supplied reviews establish the importance of site predictability and chemoselectivity, but do not demonstrate this full proposed capability.

Conceptual scope: the desired capability is general chemical control of a selected bond transformation, potentially delivered by a family of catalysts and predictive selection rules rather than one catalyst. Unactivated C(sp3)–H bonds are a central target. Aromatic C–H chemistry provides relevant context, but success at an aromatic site does not by itself demonstrate control over an unactivated C(sp3)–H site. Demonstrating one stated transformation would establish a narrower capability than installing any desired group at any chosen position.

significance.text: Predictable access to a selected C–H bond would expand synthetic planning. Chemists could plan routes around converting a bond already present in a carbon skeleton into a new functional connection, creating additional retrosynthetic disconnections and potentially avoiding some pre-functionalization steps. The 2025 review identifies streamlined, atom-economical synthesis from simpler starting materials as a benefit of C(sp3)–H functionalization. Extending that benefit reliably to chemist-selected sites in complex molecules is the revolutionary prospect.

More flexible late-stage diversification could allow an existing complex molecule to serve as the starting point for multiple derivatives, instead of requiring a substantially redesigned synthesis for each variant. Pharmaceutical and natural-product chemistry are plausible beneficiaries because the 2023 review explicitly discusses direct functionalization of these complex targets. Shorter routes and easier exploration of molecular variants remain conditional benefits: they depend on useful yields, accessible reagents, functional-group tolerance, stereochemical control and practical reaction conditions.

Impact synthesis: routine diversification across drugs and natural products would require substantially broader validation than success with one transformation on one test panel. A useful method might shorten some routes while offering little advantage for others. This concept does not require a single catalyst that replaces every enzyme or also solves methane oxidation; those are separate capabilities with additional constraints.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability targeted here is reliable, prospective control over which unactivated C–H bond reacts in a crowded molecular environment. The 2023 review documents regioselectivity and chemoselectivity challenges as molecules acquire dense and diverse functional groups. It also identifies increasing risks of catalyst intolerance and limited applicability as functional groups and potentially Lewis-basic heteroatoms accumulate. A broadly useful method must therefore combine site selection with compatibility across the surrounding molecule, rather than solve either requirement in isolation.

The 2025 abstract describes non-directed activation, transiently directed activation and activation directed by native functionality, alongside photoredox catalysis and organocatalysis. These approaches provide different ways to obtain reactivity and selectivity. The engineering goal is to turn such capabilities into dependable instructions for a preselected site, with an explicit account of where each approach succeeds or fails. Their enumeration supports the existence of a varied toolkit; it does not prove that every approach is case-specific or that no sufficiently general method exists.

Synthesis of the remaining requirements: a convincing system would need to predict both the desired outcome and important competing outcomes before experimentation, deliver enough desired product to be useful, and control relevant stereochemistry. It would also need to define its operating limits, including acceptable reaction conditions and any substrate-specific preparation. These requirements describe the proposed breakthrough; the supplied abstracts neither establish that they have all been met nor establish their universal absence as of November 1, 2026.

current_state.text: The 2023 Chemical Reviews survey by Docherty, Larrosa and colleagues, reported in the supplied research as published June 28, 2023 in volume 123, pages 7692–7760, documents progress in direct metal-catalyzed C–C bond formation within complex targets. Its abstract specifically includes alkylation, methylation, arylation and olefination. This is evidence of substantial existing chemistry, alongside documented limits in regioselectivity, chemoselectivity and catalyst tolerance. The review concerns broader C–H chemistry, so its entire scope should not be treated as demonstrations of selected unactivated C(sp3)–H functionalization.

The 2025 Chemical Society Reviews article, “Unified approaches in transition metal catalyzed C(sp3)–H functionalization,” surveys photoredox catalysis, organocatalysis, non-directed C–H activation, transiently directed activation and native-functionality-directed activation. These are established research strategies described by a review, rather than a demonstration in the supplied material of one general reaction. The research gives January 22, 2025 as the publication date; the retained bibliographic alternative gives a February 17, 2025 issue date and volume 54(4), pages 2006–2053. The supplied material does not resolve the relationship between those dates.

The evidence available through the supplied review is partial. The 2023 PubMed record provided an abstract and figure captions; the full review and figures were not inspected. The source indexed under the ACS PDF URL actually retained a matching Manchester Research Explorer abstract page, so the earlier attribution to PDF section 1.1 is unverified. For the 2025 RSC article, the retained alternative was a matching PubMed abstract record. That record lists two corrections whose contents were unavailable, leaving their relevance to these conclusions undetermined.

Evidence boundary: the supplied review contains no freshness-search results assessing developments after these publications. It therefore supports dated descriptions of progress and challenges, rather than a comprehensive determination of the field on November 1, 2026. No quantitative demonstration of the full proposed capability is supplied. The earlier assertions about chain-walking limitations and strained metallacycles explaining difficult para-selective aromatic functionalization are not established by the retained texts; that evidence gap does not show that either assertion is false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed initial demonstration: evaluate a method prospectively on a blinded panel of polyfunctional molecules, each containing several competing unactivated C–H sites. Specify the target site and one stated transformation before testing. The selected site should be the major site of that transformation, common polar groups should be tolerated, and the process should avoid installing a permanent directing group. These are proposed benchmark choices, not established community standards; perfect selectivity is not required.
completion_criteria.label: Preselected C–H sites dominate functionalization across a blinded polyfunctional panel

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reporting requirements: define panel composition, substrate-selection rules and success criteria in advance. Report desired-product yield, site selectivity, competing functional-group reactions, relevant stereochemical outcomes, failures and reaction conditions. A major-site result alone is insufficient if very little useful product forms. Disclose any temporary directing-group steps, reliance on native directing functionality, catalyst changes or substrate-specific optimization so that the practical burden and degree of predictability can be assessed.
completion_criteria.label: Report reaction outcomes and practical burdens under predefined success criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and breadth requirements: independent laboratories should reproduce representative successes and limitations using the disclosed procedures. Testing should include several preselected positions on suitable individual molecules where feasible, as well as chemically diverse substrates, to distinguish selectable-site control from repeated exploitation of one favorable site class. Success would establish demonstrated breadth for the tested transformations and conditions. Broader claims about group installation, stereochemical control, scale or routine late-stage use would require additional demonstrations; finite testing cannot establish literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Independent laboratories reproduce selectable-site control and its demonstrated chemical breadth

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — CHM-01, “A method that predicts realistic chemical outcomes before the experiment”: predictive chemistry could help select catalysts and conditions for the target C–H bond and anticipate competing reactions. The distinction is between predicting an outcome and physically achieving the selected transformation. Accurate predictions of failure would advance CHM-01 without completing CHM-11.

Roster-based synthesis — CHM-04, “Practical, on-demand synthesis of arbitrary stable molecules”: reliable selected-site functionalization could expand the reactions available to an automated or on-demand synthesis system. CHM-11 concerns control of a particular bond transformation; CHM-04 concerns the broader ability to make requested molecules, which also requires route planning and execution of other steps.

Roster-based synthesis — CHM-05, “Enzyme-level catalysts on request for arbitrary reactions”: a catalyst designed on demand, potentially an enzyme, could be one implementation of selected-site C–H functionalization. CHM-11 does not prescribe the catalyst type, and a successful implementation would not establish catalyst availability for arbitrary reactions. These comparisons use the supplied roster titles; full records for CHM-04 and CHM-05 were not supplied.

Roster-based synthesis — CHM-12, “Selective conversion of methane to methanol at useful conversion under mild conditions”: both concepts involve selective C–H transformation. Their central selectivity problems differ. CHM-11 targets a chosen position among competing sites in a complex molecule, whereas CHM-12 targets a particular conversion of methane with useful conversion and mild conditions. Completion of either would not establish the other.

Roster-based synthesis — CHM-10, “Positional chemical manufacture of macroscopic, atomically specified matter”: choosing a reaction site within a molecule has a conceptual connection to positional chemical control. CHM-11 remains a molecular synthesis capability and would not demonstrate macroscopic manufacture of atomically specified structures.

unresolved_issues: Developments after the supplied 2023 and 2025 reviews remain unassessed; the evidence does not determine whether the full capability exists as of November 1, 2026.
The contents and relevance of the two corrections listed for the 2025 review are unknown.

The ACS PDF section 1.1 locator, chain-walking limitations and proposed strained-metallacycle explanation for para-selectivity are not verified by the retained material.

brief.title: Changing a chosen bond in a complex molecule
possible: Chemists could take an existing drug or natural molecule and change a chosen carbon–hydrogen bond, including one that does not readily react. They could predict where the change would happen while preserving the molecule’s other useful features.
why: Drug researchers could make more variants of a complex molecule without redesigning its synthesis each time. Chemists could also plan shorter routes by changing bonds already present, avoiding some steps needed to prepare a molecule for further reactions.

sources.who: Jamie H Docherty, Igor Larrosa and colleagues
sources.showed: Their review describes reactions that directly form carbon–carbon bonds in complex molecules. It identifies persistent difficulties in choosing the reaction site and preserving other parts of the molecule.
sources.quote: However, challenges of regio- and chemoselectivity have emerged with application to highly complex molecules bearing significant functional group density and diversity.
sources.cited_for: Existing methods can modify complex molecules, but controlling where they react remains difficult.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate general, predictable control over a chemist’s chosen unreactive carbon–hydrogen bond.

sources.who: Jamie H Docherty, Igor Larrosa and colleagues
sources.showed: A later version of the same work.

sources.who: Jagrit Grover, Debabrata Maiti and colleagues
sources.showed: Their review surveys ways to change normally unreactive carbon–hydrogen bonds, including approaches that use existing molecular features to guide the reaction.
sources.cited_for: A varied toolkit exists for directly changing these bonds and reducing preparatory steps.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate a general system that predicts and delivers a reaction at a preselected site in complex molecules.

shown: The reviews by Docherty and colleagues and Grover and colleagues describe methods for directly changing carbon–hydrogen bonds, including examples in complex molecules. Researchers have achieved selective reactions, but these reviews do not demonstrate dependable selection of a chosen unreactive bond across diverse complex molecules.
missing: A broad demonstration would need to predict the chosen reaction site and important competing reactions before experiments begin.
The reactions would need to produce useful amounts while preserving other useful features and controlling the product’s spatial arrangement where needed.
The system would need clear operating limits and independent reproduction across diverse molecules and selectable positions.

milestones.label: Chosen sites dominate across a blinded molecule panel
milestones.explanation: A blinded test would need the preselected reaction to favor chosen unreactive bonds across molecules with competing sites, without permanent guiding attachments. This would test site control while preserving common chemical features.

milestones.label: Results and practical burdens meet predefined criteria
milestones.explanation: Tests would need predefined selection and success rules, reporting product amounts, reaction sites, side reactions, spatial arrangements, failures, conditions and preparation. This would establish usefulness and practical burden.

milestones.label: Independent laboratories reproduce selectable sites and chemical breadth
milestones.explanation: Independent laboratories would need to reproduce successes and limits across diverse molecules and, where feasible, chosen positions within a molecule. This would distinguish selectable control from repeatedly using a favorable site.

uncertain: The benchmark still needs agreed choices of reactions, molecular diversity, useful product amounts, acceptable selectivity and operating conditions.
Success with a tested reaction would leave open how far control extends to other chemical changes, larger scale and routine use.

page.title: Predictive site-selective C(sp3)–H functionalization
page.definition: A reaction toolkit would transform a chemist-selected unactivated C(sp3)–H bond—a carbon–hydrogen bond at a saturated carbon without adjacent activating functionality—in a complex molecule. Its selection rules would predict the reaction site and relevant stereochemistry while preserving specified functional groups.

goal.need: Artemisinin presents nine potential oxidation sites. The catalyst comparison below shows that different derivatives can be accessed by changing site preference. Extending such control would support diversification of existing pharmaceuticals and natural products, whose functional groups also create competing reactions and catalyst incompatibilities.

figures.caption: Catalyst-dependent oxidation of one substrate, (+)-artemisinin, reported in 2013.
figures.note: Ratios compare oxidation at C10 and C9. These are results for this substrate, not general performance thresholds.

statements.body: NSF Center for Selective C-H Functionalization, described by Davies and Morton
statements.quote: to develop catalyst-controlled selective methods to enhance the synthetic potential of C-H functionalization.

statements.body: Jin-Quan Yu's research programme, with academic and pharmaceutical coauthors
statements.quote: we could manipulate any C─H bond within any organic molecule at will, and edit it to afford any bond of choosing
statements.context: The passage states the programme's aspiration; its scope includes aromatic as well as aliphatic C–H bonds.

completion.title: Independent laboratories reproduce prospective functionalization of chemist-chosen C(sp3)–H sites.
completion.criterion: For a stated transformation and explicitly bounded substrate domain spanning complex pharmaceutical and natural-product scaffolds, independent laboratories apply a disclosed toolkit to substrates and unactivated C(sp3)–H sites selected independently of its developers. Selection rules specified before target experiments deliver isolable products whose predominant functionalization site is the requested site, including alternative positions within the same molecules. Specified surrounding functionality and stereochemistry are preserved or transformed as predicted. Success establishes the capability within the tested domain.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no external completion benchmark was found.
completion.basis: Searches covered CCHF programme statements, the Yu programme's published challenges, IUPAC-related criteria, prizes, roadmaps and C–H selectivity benchmarks. They yielded no shared completion test specifying substrate breadth, yield, selectivity and prospective accuracy. This proposed test confines the goal to one transformation and a declared domain, combining demonstrated catalyst control with prospective selection and independent reproduction.

milestones.title: A reaction preferentially functionalizes one methylene C–H site in trans-decalin.
milestones.criterion: Differentiate the competing unactivated methylene sites in trans-decalin, a published benchmark for intermolecular aliphatic C–H functionalization. Carestia and colleagues reported chlorination of this one substrate with N-chloroamide 6 at 65 °C, using one equivalent of substrate: the methylene products formed in a 7.2:1 ratio and 76% combined yield. The convention is discrimination in this benchmark; it supplies no universal numerical pass mark.
milestones.set_by: Community use of trans-decalin as a selectivity benchmark, documented and compared across reaction systems by Carestia, Ravelli and Alexanian in Chemical Science.
milestones.threshold_quote: We commenced our studies with the functionalization of trans decalin, a benchmark substrate used in studies of intermolecular, aliphatic C–H functionalizations.

milestones.title: Changing the catalyst reverses the predominant unactivated C–H reaction site in a complex molecule.
milestones.criterion: With the substrate unchanged, changing the catalyst makes a previously minor unactivated C–H functionalization site the major site. Gormisky and White demonstrated this catalyst-control test on one artemisinin substrate with Fe(PDP) and Fe(CF3-PDP), as quantified in the goal table. This establishes selectable alternatives in that molecule, without establishing access to every site.
milestones.set_by: Gormisky and White's 2013 JACS study applies reversal of inherent site preference as the catalyst-control test; reagent-controlled reversal is also used by Carestia and colleagues.
milestones.threshold_quote: override the inherent site-selectivity of oxidation to favor an alternate site.

milestones.title: A prospective toolkit delivers requested C(sp3)–H sites across its declared complex-molecule scope.
milestones.criterion: For one transformation, a developing laboratory applies fixed selection rules to previously untested complex substrates and requested unactivated C(sp3)–H sites, including alternative positions within the same molecules. The requested site predominates in isolable products with the predicted functional-group compatibility and stereochemistry throughout the declared test scope. Independent reproduction remains the completion step. Related progress includes a 2025 prediction workflow experimentally tested on five complex substrates and a 2026 decatungstate study modelling site reactivity; neither establishes this integrated result.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback: searches of programme goals, catalyst-control studies and prediction benchmarks found no shared test combining prospective site choice, chemical breadth and product formation.

not_found: No external completion benchmark or shared integrated milestone test was found for prospective chemist-chosen unactivated C(sp3)–H functionalization across complex molecules.
No agreed minimum yield, site-selectivity ratio, substrate-panel composition or prospective prediction accuracy was found for that capability.
The supplied ACS PDF and RSC review page returned HTTP 403; the 2023 review was accessible through PMC.

results.finding: Chlorination of one substrate, trans-decalin, favored one methylene site by 7.2:1.
results.detail: With one equivalent of substrate and N-chloroamide 6 at 65 °C, the methylene products had a 76% combined yield.
results.quote: Performing the reaction with 1 equiv. of substrate provided the products in a 7.2 : 1 ratio in 76% combined yield (entry 8).

results.finding: One artemisinin substrate: changing the catalyst reversed selectivity to 11:1 in favor of C9 over C10.
results.detail: Fe(PDP) favored C10 over C9 by 2:1; Fe(CF3-PDP) favored C9 over C10 by 11:1.
results.quote:
Gratifyingly, (S,S)-2
dramatically turns over the substrate controlled selectivity seen
with (S,S)-1, oxidizing at the C9 site in an 11:1 C9:C10 ratio and
furnishing 52% yield of (+)-23.

results.finding: For 1 progesterone substrate, W12M5 made C12β hydroxylation predominant at 97.7% selectivity.
results.detail: In three biological replicates, wild-type CYP68J5_fg favored C15α over C12β; W12M5 reversed that preference. W15M4 instead favored C15α at 99.6% selectivity.
results.quote:
Variant W12M5 boosted the C12
β
selectivity from 37.1% (for WT) to 97.7% with 82.3% substrate conversion (only 28.1% for WT).

results.finding: A C(sp3)–H oxidation prediction workflow correctly ranked the reactive site in 4 of 5 experimentally tested complex substrates.
results.detail: The workflow predicts innate reactivity rather than delivering requested alternative sites. One substrate was mispredicted; the study does not establish the required functional-group compatibility and stereochemistry across a declared scope.
results.quote:
Gratifyingly, we observe that on four of the five targets, the
model scores the reactive sites correctly, and the AFs provide stable,
accurate predictions at smaller data set sizes than random selection.

results.finding: A TBADT selectivity model ranked the observed functionalization site highest in 3 of 3 complex scaffolds.
results.detail: The model was applied to previously unseen scaffolds, but the text does not establish a prospective test on requested alternative sites, predicted stereochemistry, or functional-group compatibility across a declared scope.
results.quote: In all three cases, the experimentally observed site of functionalization was assigned the highest predicted probability.
